text:
Evidence supports perturbation probes as robustness diagnostics, but does not establish them as predictors of future accuracy gains. [Cascade-guided adversarial training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.05492) improves both ranking accuracy and resistance to item-replacement perturbations across four datasets; this evaluates a training intervention, not whether baseline sensitivity predicts its benefit. [FINEST](https://sejoonoh.github.io/files/FINEST_FAccTRec_2023.pdf) improves rank-list stability while preserving next-item accuracy, reinforcing that stability and accuracy are distinct outcomes. Neither result establishes that history deletion/shuffling sensitivity justifies an optimistic improvement estimate for NextItNet.

Sampled-negative margins need similar caution. [Krichene and Rendle](https://ijcai.org/proceedings/2021/651) show sampled ranking metrics can reverse model comparisons relative to full-catalog evaluation, even in expectation. Here, retain the mandated 99-negative evaluator, but interpret diagnostics within that protocol. Mathematically, positive score rescaling enlarges raw margins without changing ranks or HR@10; margin growth alone therefore cannot demonstrate improvement. Practical inference under the fixed budget: use a small, fixed validation subset for perturbation probes, measure target-rank changes and top-10 overlap, and test any proposed intervention through a matched-budget controlled ablation. The literature found supports inexpensive troubleshooting value, not a validated sensitivity-to-improvement relationship or a high potential rating without measured validation gains.
